Final rating: 4. Borderline Accept/ 4: Borderline Accept/ 5:  Accept/ 4: Borderline Accept. The paper introduces InfiniPot-V, a training-free, query-agnostic KV-cache framework for streaming video that enforces a fixed memory cap by pruning temporally redundant tokens (TaR) and retaining semantically important ones (VaN). It reduces peak memory by up to 94%, sustains real-time generation, and matches or exceeds full-cache accuracy across multiple MLLMs and long/streaming benchmarks, enabling on-device video assistants.

Reviewers agreed the paper tackles a key practical bottleneck for on-device MLLMs (e.g., real-time video assistants) and demonstrates strong engineering pragmatism. However, they questioned thin novelty (TaR parallels LongVU’s “drop static frames”; VaN echoes high-entropy/importance heuristics), shallow comparisons (only ReKV on RVS; not SOTA), and weak ablations lacking simple baselines. They also flagged robustness/scope gaps—improving Qwen2-VL but hurting Qwen2.5-VL; heuristics brittle under rapid cuts or subtle cues; English-only, controlled settings; no edge-device validation; no audio/text KV handling—plus missing broader token-reduction baselines, unclear notation, and absent hardware compatibility/deployment examples.

After the rebuttal, reviewers indicated their concerns were satisfactorily addressed and leaned toward acceptance. The ACs concur, citing the work’s practical impact and the technical soundness of a training-free, query-agnostic framework with complementary TaR and VaN. Therefore, the area chairs agree to accept the paper and recommend the authors refine it according to the reviewers’ suggestions for the camera-ready version.

We sincerely thank all reviewers for their thorough and constructive feedback throughout the review process. We are encouraged by the consistently positive feedbacks of our work.

**Key Strengths Recognized by Reviewers:**
- Practical Impact: All reviewers acknowledged the critical importance of addressing memory constraints for on-device streaming video understanding
- Technical Soundness: Reviewers praised our training-free, query-agnostic framework with complementary TaR and VaN metrics
- Comprehensive Evaluation: Strong recognition for our robust evaluation across multiple MLLMs and diverse OVU/SVU benchmarks
- Engineering Excellence: Significant memory reduction (up to 94%) with minimal performance degradation consistently highlighted

**Successfully Addressed Concerns:**
- Novelty & Technical Contribution: Demonstrated fundamental differences between our KV cache-level approach and existing vision token reduction methods through detailed ablation studies
- Robustness Analysis: Provided comprehensive edge case evaluation showing adaptive performance across different video subtasks
- Real-world Deployment: Delivered NVIDIA Jetson Orin deployment results demonstrating practical feasibility on resource-constrained devices
- Baseline Comparisons and New Benchmark: Extended evaluation with additional vision token reduction methods (Entropy, Key Filter) and new streaming video understanding benchmark (StreamingBench)

**Positive Reviewer Feedback During Rebuttal:**  
Reviewers #2, #3, and #4 explicitly confirmed "no additional concerns" and maintained their positive ratings. Reviewer #1 acknowledged our thorough responses and expressed "increasing rating" based on our commitment to broader SVU evaluations.

**Moving Forward:**    
We commit to incorporating all discussed improvements in our revision, particularly expanding SVU baseline comparisons (SVBench, OVBench) and including the comprehensive analyses developed during rebuttal discussions. These enhancements will strengthen our contribution to bridging the gap between streaming video understanding research and real-world edge deployment.

Thank you for taking the time to review our rebuttal and providing additional constructive feedback. We are pleased that our clarifications regarding *TaR/VaN's fundamental differences* from existing methods, and our *additional streaming video benchmark results*, have addressed your initial concerns. We sincerely appreciate your continued engagement in improving our work. Our responses to your remaining comments are as follows.

---

**1. Qwen2.5-VL-3B EgoSchema Performance Analysis**

Thank you for highlighting the EgoSchema performance degradation in Qwen2.5VL. We observe in `Table 1` that the 2.5VL series demonstrates higher absolute performance than the 2VL series (2.5VL-7B Full: 67.6, 2VL-7B Full: 65.6) but exhibits relatively higher sensitivity to KV compression (2.5VL-7B: 67.6→65.8, 2VL-7B: 65.2→65.6), with this sensitivity becoming more pronounced in smaller model sizes (2.5VL-3B: 64.4→61.8) likely due to reduced model capacity affecting resilience to KV cache compression. 

However, as shown in the `Table R3` below, our method consistently outperforms all baseline compression methods (Key Filter, entropy, and uniform) across different cache budgets by up to 3%. (56.8 vs 60.2) Moreover, the performance gap to full KV cache closes substantially at 12K (64.2 vs 64.4), demonstrating that our approach can achieve more robust compression even with models that show varying resilience characteristics. We will continue to investigate the relative performance differences observed in smaller models on EgoSchema to better understand this phenomenon.

| Qwen2.5-VL-3B | 3K | 6K | 12K | Full |
|--------|----|----|-----|------|
| Uniform | 56.8 | 60.2 | 63.2 | 64.4 |
| Key Filter | 58.8 | 60.9 | 63.4 | 64.4 |
| Entropy | 57.6 | 60.6 | 63.6 | 64.4 |
| TaR + VaN (Ours) | **60.2** | **61.8** | **64.2** | 64.4 |

*Table R3. EgoSchema accuracy comparison across different KV cache budgets and compression methods (Full: 50K)*

---

**2. Streaming Video Understanding Baseline Comparisons**

We appreciate the reviewer's valuable suggestions for broader baseline comparisons. We would like to emphasize that InfiniPot-V proposes a *training-free* method that uses *fixed memory* for streaming video processing in memory-constrained environments such as edge devices (e.g., Jetson Orin). We respectfully observe that [a. VideoLLM-online, c. VideoChat-Online] focus on training specialized online video LLMs, while [b. StreamChat] employs hierarchical external memory systems, which are not directly compatible with training-free memory-constrained scenarios.

However, the papers you cited indeed important works in streaming video understanding, and we acknowledge their significance. While direct comparisons are challenging due to time and resource constraints, in our revision, we will expand our evaluation to include the benchmarks from these works (b. StreamBench, c. OVBench) and provide accuracy comparisons with training-based online video LLMs (a. VideoLLM-online c. VideoChat-online) and external memory based LLM (b. StreamChat) to better position our training-free/memory-constrained approach within the broader streaming video understanding landscape.

Thank you for highlighting these important references that will strengthen our work's positioning and evaluation comprehensiveness. We hope our additional responses address your remaining concerns, and please let us know if you have any further comments or questions.

Moreover, the paper still lacks comparisons with a broader set of streaming video–understanding methods. Although the topic centers on streaming video, the experiments include only ReKV as a baseline. More published open-source approaches—e.g., [a], [b], [c]—should be considered; relying on a single baseline is not sufficient.

[a] Chen, Joya, et al. "Videollm-online: Online video large language model for streaming video." CVPR 2024.

[b] Xiong, Haomiao, et al. "Streaming video understanding and multi-round interaction with memory-enhanced knowledge." ICLR 2025.

> **Layer-Adaptive PoolSize assignment based on CV:**

This approach differs from LongVU's input vision token compression that forces *identical token eviction across all KV cache layers.*

**VaN establishes Value norm as a semantic importance proxy through intermediate layer analysis.** We conduct entropy analysis of vision tokens at each intermediate layer by projecting their hidden states, demonstrating that tokens with higher Value norms consistently exhibit higher entropy and better preserve long video accuracy when retained (see `Fig.3`). This provides concrete evidence that L2 norms of Value embeddings serve as effective semantic importance scores, complemented by our layer-wise adaptive pooling technique. Unlike Top-K Entropy selection that operates at the token level using final vocabulary projections, VaN compresses based on L2 norms of Value embeddings at each attention layer.

**Ablation study with suggested alternatives confirms the superiority of our approach.** `Table R1` shows that replacing TaR with LongVU's Key Filter results in nearly 4% performance degradation (64.5→60.8), while replacing VaN with Top-K Entropy selection leads to nearly 3% performance drop (63.0→60.2). These results demonstrate that our KV cache compression enables more temporally meaningful token retention and semantically important token preservation across attention heads compared to the suggested alternatives.


---

> **Weakness 2.** Comparative study on streaming video understanding is shallow: only ReKV is benchmarked, limited to a single dataset (RVS), and the method does not reach the current SOTA there. Broader baselines and benchmarks in SVU are missing.

summary.value: InfiniPot-V introduces a continual KV-cache compression framework that keeps GPU memory usage constant regardless of video length. When the cache reaches a user-set budget, the system compresses it by (i) pruning temporally redundant patches via Temporal-axis Redundancy (TaR) and (ii) preserving semantically salient regions via Value-Norm (VaN). The method is training-free and query-agnostic; across four open-source MLLMs and six benchmarks, it slashes peak memory by up to 94 % while sustaining real-time 14 fps generation and matching or surpassing full-cache accuracy.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
1. Straightforward, training-free cache compression that can be plugged into existing MLLMs without retraining.
 2. Consistent memory reduction (≈ 94 %) across four backbone models with only marginal speed overhead, proving the engineering practicality.
 3. Paper is clearly written; algorithmic steps and ablation studies are easy to follow, which aids reproducibility.

Weaknesses
1. Claimed novelty is thin. The Temporal-axis Redundancy module repeats the “drop static frames” idea already seen in recent work such as LongVU; VaN likewise relies on a well-known “high-entropy tokens carry more information” intuition, and the layer-wise pooling tweak is incremental.
2. Comparative study on streaming video understanding is shallow: only ReKV is benchmarked, limited to a single dataset (RVS), and the method does not reach the current SOTA there. Broader baselines and benchmarks in SVU are missing.
3. Method improves Qwen2-VL on EgoSchema yet hurts Qwen-2.5-VL noticeably, raising doubts about robustness; the paper offers no analysis for this drop.
4. The ablation study is not strong enough. More simple strategies should be compared. For example, add an ablation that replaces TaR with LongVU’s key-similarity filter and replaces VaN with a simple top-k entropy selection. Show accuracy and memory for each variant.

summary.value: This paper introduces InfiniPot-V, a novel framework designed to address the critical problem of unbounded key-value (KV) cache growth in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) during streaming video understanding. The authors propose the first training-free, query-agnostic compression framework that enforces a hard, length-independent memory budget, making it suitable for resource-constrained edge devices. The core method, termed Continual KV cache Compression (CKV), monitors the cache size during video stream processing and, upon reaching a user-defined threshold, performs an efficient in-place compression. This compression is guided by two lightweight, complementary metrics: Temporal-axis Redundancy (TaR) to prune temporally redundant tokens and Value-Norm Importance (VaN) to preserve semantically salient tokens. The authors demonstrate that InfiniPot-V can be applied as a plug-and-play module to various MLLMs, significantly reducing peak memory usage while maintaining or even surpassing the accuracy of full-cache baselines across multiple long-video and streaming benchmarks.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Strengths:**

* **Significance and Originality:** The paper tackles a crucial and practical bottleneck for deploying MLLMs on edge devices for real-world applications like real-time video assistants. It introduces what appears to be the first framework to enforce a truly fixed memory budget for streaming video understanding in a query-agnostic and training-free manner. The proposed TaR and VaN metrics provide an elegant and lightweight solution that contrasts sharply with existing methods that are often query-dependent, require full cache materialization, or necessitate costly retraining.
* **Quality and Performance:** The work is technically strong and validated with impressive empirical results. InfiniPot-V demonstrates remarkable efficiency, achieving up to 94% peak GPU memory reduction with only a 0.5% latency overhead. Across four open-source MLLMs and six benchmarks, it consistently matches or exceeds the accuracy of full-cache baselines, showcasing that significant compression can be achieved with minimal performance degradation. The thorough ablation studies effectively validate the synergy between the TaR and VaN components.
* **Practicality and Impact:** The plug-and-play and training-free nature of InfiniPot-V makes it highly practical and likely to have a significant impact on the field. By eliminating the need for retraining and CPU offloading, it provides a viable path toward deploying powerful video understanding models on consumer devices like smartphones and AR glasses, bridging a critical gap between large-scale research models and real-world applications.

**Weaknesses:**

* **Quality/Robustness of Compression Heuristics:** The proposed compression criteria have potential weaknesses in certain scenarios. The TaR metric, which relies on identifying temporal redundancy, may be less effective for videos with constant, rapid scene changes or frequent edits where static content is minimal. Similarly, the VaN metric, which uses the $\ell_2$ norm of Value vectors as a proxy for semantic importance, could potentially discard low-norm but contextually critical visual cues, such as small text overlays or subtle but important objects. The robustness of these heuristics across more diverse and challenging video styles is not fully explored.
* **Scope of Evaluation and Generalization:** The evaluation, while extensive, has some gaps. The benchmarks used are primarily in English, leaving the framework's performance on multilingual content unevaluated. Furthermore, the experiments are conducted under controlled conditions (e.g., fixed frame rates), and the system's robustness in more challenging, real-world scenarios like low-light conditions, occlusions, or dynamic frame rates remains unvalidated. The experiments are also conducted on high-end A100 GPUs, with no deployment validation on the target edge devices (e.g., Jetson Orin), leaving questions about real-world latency and power consumption unanswered.
* **Limited Multimodal Scope:** The current framework focuses exclusively on compressing the visual modality's KV cache. In many real-world videos, audio and transcribed speech are critical parallel streams of information. The paper does not address how to integrate or co-compress audio or text-based KV caches, which would be essential for a truly holistic understanding of multimodal streams.

questions.value:
1.  **Robustness Under Challenging Conditions:** How does InfiniPot-V perform on videos that challenge its core assumptions? For example, how does TaR handle high-motion sports videos with minimal static background, and can VaN reliably preserve small but crucial textual information on screen? Have you considered adaptive thresholds for TaR and VaN to mitigate potential failures in such adverse conditions?
2.  **Hardware-Specific Performance:** The paper demonstrates impressive efficiency on A100 GPUs. To fully validate its practicality for edge computing, could you provide latency and power consumption metrics on representative ARM-based devices like a smartphone SoC or NVIDIA Jetson?
3.  **Extending to Multimodal Streams:** A key area for future work is multimodal compression. How do you envision extending InfiniPot-V to jointly handle visual, audio, and synchronized text (e.g., subtitles) streams? Would this require new cross-modal redundancy metrics to decide which modality's tokens to preserve, or could each stream be compressed independently?
4.  **Long-Term Semantic Retention:** For ultra-long videos, such as hour-long surveillance footage, repeatedly compressing the KV cache might lead to the gradual decay of important semantic information from early in the stream ("catastrophic forgetting" in the cache). Have you analyzed this effect? Would a hierarchical caching mechanism (e.g., storing summaries of older, heavily compressed blocks) be a potential solution to ensure long-term memory retention?

summary.value: In this paper, InfiniPot-V algorithm, which is the training-free KV cache compression method, is proposed for streaming video understanding. The proposed algorithm employs two techniques, TaR and VaN, to keep the KV cache within a certain memory limit. Specifically, TaR measures the temporal redundancy score of each patch in past frames and remove the redundant patches. VaN is the metric for token-level semantic importance, which is actually L2norm of value embedding. The proposed algorithm keeps the tokens with high VaN scores (after pooling) in the memory. The experimental results including extensive analysis show that the proposed algorithm achieves comparable or better performances than conventional algorithms.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
> **Strength**
* This paper is well-written and easy to follow.
* This paper demonstrates the validity of the design of the proposed algorithm through various empirical analyses. Furthermore, by applying the proposed method to different MLLMs and evaluating their performances on multiple benchmark datasets, it shows the effectiveness of the proposed InfiniPot-V.
* The proposed algorithm is a practical solution that can be easily applied to existing MLLMs to enable memory-efficient inference. It achieves a better computation-performance trade-off compared to existing approaches. Moreover, the paper provides a detailed explanation of the method to ensure reproducibility.

> **Weakness**
* While the proposed method seems simple and effective, the proposed scoring methods are not particularly novel.
* The mathematical notation could be improved for better clarity.

questions.value:
The proposed algorithm may have the potential to support memory-efficient inference across various MLLMs, depending on their intended use and deployment environment. However, it would be even more compelling if the following aspects can be further improved. Of course, I would also be interested in hearing the authors' thoughts on my questions.

---

* L159, the definition of $H$ seems to be missing, although its meaning can be inferred from the context.

* Figure 2 (b) compares the static patch similarities of keys and values. It is useful, but it would also be beneficial to compare the key similarity of non-static patches. This could demonstrate that static and non-static patches can be effectively distinguished based on $s^{TaR}$.

* Table 4 shows the ablation study results. There seems to be many alternative designs worth comparing in addition to VaN Reverse. For example, instead of using TopK selection, it is possible to select tokens at fixed intervals after sorting them by scores. It may also be possible to identify important frames by computing the average VaN score for each frame, and then select a different number of tokens from each frame based on its importance. While Top-K selection is simple and effective, it would be interesting to see additional comparative experiments with other alternative methods.

* It would be helpful to visualize the selection results based on the actual scores. This would provide an intuitive understanding of how effectively the proposed method identifies important tokens.


* Typo (minor)
1. There is a mixed use of $K_{recent}, V_{recent}$  and $K_\textrm{recent}, V_\textrm{recent}$ (e.g. Algorithm 1 and Eq.4)
2. Similarly, $s^{VaN}$ and $s^{TaR}$ are also used with inconsistent notation. (e.g. Algorithm 1, Eq. 4, and L181)
3. Figure 2 (c) VaN (spatial) -> VaN (Spatial), for consistency in capitalization.

summary.value: The paper introduces InfiniPot-V, a novel framework designed to address memory constraints in streaming video understanding (SVU) by compressing the key-value (KV) cache in a training-free, query-agnostic manner. Unlike traditional offline video understanding methods that assume access to the entire video, InfiniPot-V processes arbitrarily long video streams in real-time, maintaining a fixed memory footprint. The framework employs two complementary metrics: Temporal-axis Redundancy (TaR), which prunes redundant tokens based on cosine similarity across time, and Value-Norm Importance (VaN), which prioritizes tokens based on the L2 norm of their Value vectors for semantic salience. InfiniPot-V achieves significant memory reduction (down to 6K tokens for 6K token contexts) while maintaining accuracy comparable to or better than existing methods.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
- The paper presents a robust evaluation across diverse benchmarks (VideoMME, EgoSchema, MLVU, LongVideoBench, RVS Ego, RVS Movie), covering both offline and streaming tasks.
- InfiniPot-V addresses a critical bottleneck in deploying SVU on memory-constrained devices, a pressing issue as video-based multimodal assistants become more prevalent.
- The introduction of TaR and VaN as complementary compression metrics is novel, particularly in the context of streaming video. 

Weaknesses:
- More comparisons with previous works on reducing the number of vision tokens in LMMs should be included to enhance the completeness of the experiments.
- While the framework’s focus on on-device deployment is significant, the paper does not discuss compatibility with specific hardware (e.g., mobile GPUs or TPUs) or provide real-world deployment examples.

questions.value:
- How does InfiniPot-V perform in edge cases, such as videos with minimal temporal redundancy (e.g., highly dynamic scenes) or low semantic variance (e.g., static backgrounds)? Are there scenarios where TaR or VaN might fail to preserve critical information?
-  The paper mentions a “layer-adaptive pooling strategy” in the VaN metric but provides limited details on its implementation. How is the pooling intensity determined for each layer, and what factors (e.g., model architecture, token distribution) influence this adaptation?

title.value: InfiniPot-V: Memory-Constrained KV Cache Compression for Streaming Video Understanding

TLDR.value: InfiniPot-V presents KV-cache control framework for streaming input video processing with fixed memory usage

abstract.value: Modern multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can reason over hour-long video, yet their key–value (KV) cache grows linearly with time—quickly exceeding the fixed memory of phones, AR glasses, and edge robots. Prior compression schemes either assume the whole video and user query are available offline or must first build the full cache, so memory still scales with stream length. InfiniPot-V is the first training-free, query-agnostic framework that enforces a hard, length-independent memory cap for \textit{streaming} video understanding. During video encoding it monitors the cache and, once a user-set threshold is reached, runs a lightweight compression pass that (i) removes temporally redundant tokens via Temporal-axis Redundancy (TaR) metric and (ii) keeps semantically significant tokens via Value-Norm (VaN) ranking. Across four open-source MLLMs and four long-video and streaming-video benchmarks, InfiniPot-V cuts peak GPU memory by up to 94\%, sustains real-time generation, and matches or surpasses full-cache accuracy—even in multi-turn dialogues. By dissolving the KV cache bottleneck without retraining or query knowledge, InfiniPot-V closes the gap for on-device streaming video assistants.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/ ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).
